study.title: Very Early Outcomes in Endoscopic Versus Open Carpal Tunnel Release
study.journal: Journal of hand surgery global online

cover.headline: Both types of carpal tunnel surgery work. But **one gets you back to work days faster**.

slides.title: Endoscopic and open carpal tunnel release both relieve symptoms, so the choice is mostly preference.
slides.body:
Carpal tunnel release can be done through a traditional open incision or with an endoscope through a smaller cut. Both techniques decompress the nerve and eventually restore function.

The assumption is that once you account for surgeon skill and postoperative care, the two approaches deliver similar results in the first two weeks after surgery. The long-term outcomes are what matter most.

slides.title: Endoscopic patients reported less pain at day 3, day 7, and day 14 after surgery.
slides.body:
A prospective multicenter study tracked patients after carpal tunnel release using standardized postoperative care. Pain scores on both the Numeric Rating Scale and the Patient-Rated Wrist and Hand Evaluation were lower in the endoscopic group at every measured checkpoint.

Function scores also favored the endoscopic approach. Patients who had endoscopic release showed earlier return of hand function across multiple assessment tools in the first two weeks.

slides.title: Fifty percent of endoscopic patients were back at work by day 3, versus 20 percent in the open group.
slides.body:
The difference in return-to-work rates was significant at both day 3 and day 7. For people who need to meet family responsibilities or cannot afford extended time off, those extra days matter.

The gap narrowed over time, but the very early postoperative period between days 3 and 14 is when the endoscopic approach showed its clearest advantage in pain, function, and return to work.

caveats: This study found a pattern, not a cause. Something else could explain the link between technique and recovery speed.
The study does not report total sample size or how patients were assigned to each procedure.
All three surgeons were fellowship-trained hand specialists. Results may differ in other settings.

cta.sub: One real study, every weekday. The full paper is linked in bio.

caption: Endoscopic carpal tunnel release is linked to less pain and faster return to work in the first two weeks after surgery compared to the open technique. A prospective multicenter study followed patients after both procedures using standardized postoperative care. Endoscopic patients had lower pain scores at days 3, 7, and 14, better early function scores, and significantly higher rates of return to work at days 3 and 7. The study appeared in the Journal of Hand Surgery Global Online and involved three fellowship-trained hand surgeons. The abstract does not specify total sample size. Full study: doi.org/10.1016/j.jhsg.2026.101104 — Send this to someone facing carpal tunnel surgery who wants to know what those first two weeks might actually feel like.
